paragraphs: Autonomous racing asks driving algorithms to control cars close to their handling limits. Studying this with physical vehicles is expensive, while limited physics accuracy can make open-source simulators less useful for this purpose. This paper introduces a simulation platform built on Assetto Corsa to support testing, validation, and comparison of autonomous racing algorithms in realistic, challenging scenarios.

The contribution combines an environment with algorithms adapted to racing and a substantial dataset collected from human drivers. The platform accommodates reinforcement learning and classical Model Predictive Control, giving researchers a shared setting for examining different approaches to vehicle control. Human driving data adds another resource alongside the simulation itself.

The authors also evaluate algorithms in offline reinforcement learning, where learning uses previously collected experience. They publicly release the environment, benchmarks, working examples, and datasets. The paper's stated contribution is therefore research infrastructure spanning simulation, reference algorithms, and human data, making several parts of an autonomous racing study available together.
neurips-2024-a-simulation-benchmark-for-.tldr: A racing platform built on Assetto Corsa combines simulation, adapted control algorithms, and human driving data for autonomous racing research.

paragraphs: BioTrove provides a large collection of biodiversity images curated from research-grade iNaturalist observations. It contains 161.9 million images covering approximately 366,600 species across animals, fungi, and plants. Scientific names, common names, and taxonomic hierarchies accompany the images, connecting visual examples to both individual species and broader biological categories.

The authors also release CLIP models trained on BioTrove-Train, a subset of 40 million captioned images. This subset emphasizes seven groups described as underrepresented in standard image recognition models: birds, arachnids, insects, plants, fungi, mollusks, and reptiles. The training resource therefore directs attention toward organisms relevant to biodiversity and agriculture that general image collections may represent less well.

New benchmarks assess zero-shot recognition across life stages, rare species, confounding species, and different taxonomic levels. These evaluations examine several distinct recognition challenges rather than treating species identification as one uniform task. The authors anticipate applications in pest control, crop monitoring, and conservation; those uses are presented as opportunities the publicly available data and models could support.
neurips-2024-biotrove-a-large-curated-im.tldr: BioTrove releases 161.9 million curated biodiversity images, specialized CLIP models, and benchmarks for recognizing diverse organisms.

paragraphs: Vision-language compositionality benchmarks test whether models connect images with descriptions that correctly express their contents. Existing benchmarks such as SugarCrepe ask a model to choose between a correct description and a deliberately difficult incorrect one. BiVLC expands this evaluation so that matching runs in both directions: from images to text and from text to images.

The authors generate an additional image from the difficult incorrect description. Each resulting pair of images and descriptions supplies two image-to-text decisions and two text-to-image decisions. Human annotators remove ill-formed examples. This construction makes the reverse matching task part of the benchmark, exposing capabilities that image-to-text evaluation alone does not measure.

Experiments reveal particularly weak performance when models must select an image from text, and including both directions substantially changes conclusions from earlier evaluations. Training a contrastive model with synthetic images and text improves over its base model on SugarCrepe and on both BiVLC directions. A remaining gap to human performance shows that the evaluated models still struggle with this capability.
neurips-2024-bivlc-extending-vision-lang.tldr: BiVLC adds text-to-image matching to compositionality evaluation, revealing weaknesses that image-to-text benchmarks can miss.

paragraphs: Motion generation and editing systems use written instructions to produce or alter human movement. CigTime investigates the reverse task: given someone's current movement and a desired movement, produce instructions explaining how to move toward the target. Sports coaching and motor skill learning motivate this focus on corrective guidance.

The approach uses large language models to create corrective text and existing motion generation and editing frameworks to assemble training examples. Each example connects three elements: a source motion, a target motion, and an instruction describing the correction. These triplets provide supervision for a new motion-language model that generates instructions from the two motions.

This formulation matters because its output describes a change between movements rather than merely describing a movement in isolation. The authors report qualitative and quantitative results across diverse applications, with substantial improvements over baselines. Their findings support the approach's effectiveness in the instructional scenarios examined, where text provides guidance for correcting performance toward a specified target.
neurips-2024-cigtime-corrective-instruct.tldr: CigTime learns to generate corrective instructions by connecting a person's current motion, a target motion, and text describing the change.

paragraphs: Human pose estimation often locates body joints using heatmaps that assign confidence scores to image positions. Conventional methods represent these maps as pixel grids, introducing quantization error when a continuous location must be expressed on a discrete grid. The paper identifies this problem as especially damaging for low-resolution images, where heatmap methods lose much of their advantage over direct coordinate prediction.

NerPE replaces the fixed grid representation with a continuous function. Given a position within the image, it predicts joint confidence scores using surrounding image features. This formulation maintains continuity in position and confidence during training and separates the learned representation from a particular output resolution.

At inference, the same trained model can produce heatmaps at arbitrary resolutions without retraining, enabling sub-pixel localization. The authors also introduce progressive coordinate decoding to reduce computation: locating joints no longer requires generating an entire high-resolution heatmap. Together, these designs combine a continuous confidence representation with a decoding procedure that avoids evaluating every location on a dense grid.
neurips-2024-continuous-heatmap-regressi.tldr: NerPE predicts continuous joint-confidence heatmaps and progressively decodes coordinates to enable sub-pixel pose localization without full high-resolution maps.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained vision transformer using a relatively small set of learned parameters. Common approaches represent an adaptation matrix through a narrow down-projection followed by an up-projection. The paper argues that fixing this bottleneck size restricts flexibility because different layers may benefit from adaptations with different ranks.

The proposed method takes inspiration from singular value decomposition, which separates a matrix into two directional transformations and diagonal scaling values. It constructs orthogonal transformations using Householder transformations, which require only a vector to represent a transformation. This provides an economical way to build the directional parts of the adaptation matrix.

The scaling values are learned separately for each layer, allowing adaptation matrices to have varying ranks across the network. The design therefore gives layers more individual flexibility while retaining the goal of parameter-efficient adaptation. Experiments on standard downstream vision tasks show promising fine-tuning performance. The stated result supports this alternative matrix representation without asserting that it universally surpasses existing adaptation methods.
neurips-2024-efficient-adaptation-of-pre.tldr: Householder-based adaptation lets vision-transformer layers learn different adaptation ranks within a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization studies decisions made over successive rounds, with regret measuring accumulated loss relative to an optimal fixed decision. This paper shows that algorithms adaptive to loss-function curvature can also exploit the geometry of the feasible decision set. That creates another route to fast regret growth, including for convex losses.

In stochastic environments, the authors prove an O(ρ log T) bound when an optimal decision lies on the feasible boundary and the underlying loss gradient there is nonzero. Here, ρ measures the smallest enclosing sphere that includes that optimum. The result uses a local geometric property and can simultaneously exploit curvature in the loss.

The analysis also provides O(√T) regret in adversarial environments and a bound combining logarithmic growth with a corruption-dependent term in corrupted stochastic environments. These guarantees cover settings where follow-the-leader can incur linear regret. An extension to q-uniformly convex sets gives a matching upper bound interpolating between logarithmic regret for strongly convex sets and square-root regret as curvature vanishes.
neurips-2024-fast-rates-in-stochastic-on.tldr: Under stated stochastic conditions, curvature-adaptive algorithms exploit feasible-set geometry for logarithmic regret while retaining guarantees under adversarial or corrupted losses.

paragraphs: FIRE focuses on what happens after a vision-language model gives an answer: can it use user feedback to improve its response? The authors construct 1.1 million multi-turn conversations drawn from 27 source datasets. This makes feedback-driven revision an explicit training target across diverse tasks, rather than evaluating only the model's initial response.

The collection process has two stages. GPT-4V generates FIRE-100K, and models trained on that collection generate FIRE-1M. The larger component scales up the available refinement conversations using models trained on the initial data. The authors also build FIRE-Bench, comprising 11,000 test conversations, two evaluation settings, and a model that supplies feedback during evaluation.

Fine-tuning LLaVA on both dataset components produces FIRE-LLaVA. On FIRE-Bench, the authors report strong refinement capability and a 50% improvement over untrained vision-language models. This finding supports the value of specifically training models to incorporate feedback, with the aim of making user-agent interactions more efficient through better revisions.
neurips-2024-fire-a-dataset-for-feedback.tldr: FIRE supplies feedback-refinement training conversations and a benchmark, with a fine-tuned LLaVA model showing improved response revision.

paragraphs: Large language models can be expensive to run because inference involves enormous numbers of parameters. Activation sparsity offers a way to reduce this work by using only parts of the model for a given computation. Existing approaches exploit sparsity that emerges naturally after training; this paper investigates whether training can deliberately encourage more structured sparsity.

Learn-To-be-Efficient, or LTE, trains models to activate fewer neurons while balancing sparsity against task performance. Its aim is to make computational efficiency something the model learns. The method also applies to non-ReLU activation functions, including those used in LLaMA, extending beyond the ReLU-focused scope of the MoEfication methods discussed in the abstract.

Evaluations on language understanding, generation, and instruction tuning show LTE consistently outperforming the compared state-of-the-art baselines. Combined with a hardware-aware custom kernel, it reduces LLaMA2-7B inference latency by 25% at 50% sparsity. That result connects the learned reduction in active computation to measured execution speed for the reported model and implementation.
neurips-2024-learn-to-be-efficient-build.tldr: LTE trains language models to activate fewer neurons and, with a custom kernel, reduces LLaMA2-7B inference latency by 25% at 50% sparsity.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a face's texture from images becomes difficult when objects such as hats partly obscure the face and alter its illumination. Methods developed around a single, uniform lighting assumption cannot correctly handle the complicated lighting described here. The paper addresses texture modeling in these conditions, extending attention beyond well-lit faces with little external occlusion.

Its central idea, Light Decoupling, represents the observed illumination as a combination of several separate lighting conditions. Learned neural representations are combined with these conditions to imitate the complex illumination. This gives the framework a richer account of how lighting affects the visible face while it models the underlying facial texture.

Experiments on individual images and video sequences demonstrate the approach's effectiveness under challenging illumination caused by occlusions. The contribution is the change in how illumination is represented: allowing multiple lighting components provides a way to handle appearances that a single uniform light model cannot adequately describe. The reported evidence covers both still-image and sequential inputs.
neurips-2024-learning-to-decouple-the-li.tldr: Light Decoupling models complex facial illumination as multiple lighting conditions to improve 3D texture reconstruction under external occlusions.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer energy-efficient information transmission, but their task performance has lagged behind conventional artificial neural networks. This paper studies how multi-threshold spiking models relate mathematically to standard spiking models and quantized artificial neural networks. That analysis motivates a new model called LM-HT.

LM-HT uses equally spaced thresholds and can dynamically regulate the global input current and membrane-potential leakage over time. These controls expand how the spiking model handles incoming information. Through reparameterization, the model can also be expressed as a conventional single-threshold model, providing flexibility for hardware deployment.

With a special initialization, LM-HT integrates into an ANN-to-SNN conversion framework. This hybrid learning approach improves the relatively weak performance of converted networks at low time latency. Across several types of datasets, the authors report results exceeding prior state-of-the-art work and reaching performance comparable to quantized artificial neural networks. The findings connect a more flexible training model with compatibility for simpler spiking implementations.
neurips-2024-lm-ht-snn-enhancing-the-per.tldr: LM-HT combines learnable multi-threshold spiking dynamics with conversion and reparameterization to reach performance comparable to quantized artificial neural networks.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest-neighbor search retrieves vectors similar to a query and supports applications such as vector databases and retrieval-augmented generation. Clustering-based search methods scale well and suit distributed or disk-based systems, but methods using product quantization for scoring have slower queries than leading graph-based alternatives. This paper targets that scoring step.

The authors recast inner-product approximation as a supervised regression problem with multiple outputs. Reduced-rank regression then supplies an efficient way to estimate those scores. This changes how candidate similarities are computed while retaining a clustering-based search organization. The proposed scoring method is incorporated into the LoRANN search library.

On the high-dimensional datasets studied, reduced-rank regression improves both query latency and memory usage relative to product quantization. LoRANN is also competitive with leading graph-based algorithms and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art GPU search methods on high-dimensional data. These results show that improving the scoring mechanism can make clustering-based search substantially more competitive in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-lorann-low-rank-matrix-fact.tldr: LoRANN uses reduced-rank regression for similarity scoring, improving clustering-based nearest-neighbor search on high-dimensional datasets.

paragraphs: Reasoning across multiple images requires a multimodal language model to combine information from several visual inputs. MaVEn addresses the limitations of models primarily oriented toward understanding individual images. Its contribution is a visual encoding framework that represents image information at two levels of detail.

One component uses discrete visual symbols to express broad semantic concepts. The other retains continuous feature sequences that describe finer visual details. Combining these representations is intended to reduce the semantic gap between visual information and text while preserving information needed for detailed interpretation. The model can therefore draw on both coarse concepts and fine features when processing multiple images.

MaVEn also includes a dynamic reduction mechanism for long continuous feature sequences, addressing the efficiency demands of multi-image processing. Experiments show significant improvements in complex multi-image understanding and gains in single-image settings as well. The findings support combining complementary visual representations with sequence reduction, rather than treating representation quality and processing efficiency as separate concerns.
neurips-2024-maven-an-effective-multi-gr.tldr: MaVEn combines coarse visual symbols, detailed continuous features, and dynamic sequence reduction to improve multimodal image understanding.

paragraphs: Dynamic scene reconstruction must represent objects as they move over time. Extensions of 3D Gaussian Splatting to moving scenes can be difficult to optimize when they lack explicit constraints on object motion. MotionGS adds motion guidance to the deformation of the Gaussian elements used to represent the scene.

Its optical-flow module separates apparent image movement into camera flow and object-motion flow. This distinction matters because camera movement and object movement contribute differently to changes between views. The extracted motion flow constrains Gaussian deformation so that the changing representation follows dynamic objects.

A second module refines camera poses by alternating between optimizing the Gaussians and optimizing the camera estimates. This mitigates errors from inaccurate poses alongside the motion constraints. Experiments on monocular dynamic scenes report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both visual and numerical comparisons. Together, the results support explicitly separating motion sources and refining camera estimates when learning a deformable Gaussian scene representation.
neurips-2024-motiongs-exploring-explicit.tldr: MotionGS separates camera and object motion to guide deformable Gaussian reconstruction, while refining camera poses to reduce estimation errors.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe signals such as images, shapes, and audio through functions learned from sampled points. A common design asks one network to represent the entire domain. This places many global constraints on a single function, even when different parts of the signal have different local structure.

Neural Experts uses a mixture of experts to learn local, piecewise-continuous functions. The system learns both how to subdivide the domain and how to fit its parts. A gating network participates in this division, and the authors introduce conditioning and pretraining methods for that network to improve convergence toward the desired solution.

The approach can be incorporated into existing implicit-representation formulations. Evaluations on surface, image, and audio reconstruction show improvements over methods without a mixture of experts, with reported benefits in speed, accuracy, and memory requirements. The findings support distributing representation across locally fitted functions instead of placing the full reconstruction burden on a single network.
neurips-2024-neural-experts-mixture-of-e.tldr: Neural Experts jointly learns domain subdivisions and local implicit functions, improving reconstruction speed, accuracy, and memory requirements in evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: A signed distance function represents a surface through the locations where its value is zero. Learning such a function from multiple views is difficult when using 3D Gaussian Splatting because the Gaussian elements are discrete, sparse, and can drift away from the surface. This paper couples Gaussian rendering with a learned distance field to address those problems.

The method dynamically pulls the Gaussians onto the neural field's zero-level surface and renders them through differentiable rasterization. In the other direction, it updates the distance field by pulling neighboring space toward the aligned Gaussians. These linked operations progressively refine the field near the surface while making use of consistency across views.

Both the Gaussians and the neural distance function are jointly optimized using image-color and geometric constraints. The authors report more accurate, smoother, and more complete surfaces with finer geometric detail. Numerical and visual comparisons on widely used benchmarks show improvements over state-of-the-art results, supporting the benefit of keeping the rendered elements and inferred surface closely aligned.
neurips-2024-neural-signed-distance-func.tldr: Jointly aligning Gaussian elements with a neural distance field improves multi-view surface reconstruction in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Certified defenses provide formal robustness guarantees within specified attack conditions. Their practical usefulness has been constrained by the level of certified robustness attainable. This paper asks whether additional training data generated by diffusion models can improve deterministic certified defenses, extending an approach previously shown to help empirical adversarial training.

The authors find that generated data can substantially improve certified defenses, but the scaling behavior differs notably from that of empirical methods. They also provide recommendations for scaling certified training. This distinction matters because gains observed in adversarial training do not by themselves establish how methods with formal certificates will respond to additional generated data.

The approach achieves state-of-the-art deterministic certificates on CIFAR-10 for an ℓ2 threat model with ε = 36/255 and an ℓ∞ threat model with ε = 8/255. Improvements over previous results are 3.95 and 1.39 percentage points, respectively, with similar gains reported on CIFAR-100. These findings demonstrate stronger certified robustness under the specified threat models.
neurips-2024-on-the-scalability-of-certi.tldr: Diffusion-generated training data improves deterministic certified robustness, with scaling behavior that differs from empirical adversarial training.

paragraphs: Preference learning is commonly used to make language-model responses more desirable to humans. This paper examines a specific expectation: whether preference-tuned models assign greater likelihood to preferred outputs than to less preferred ones. On common preference datasets, most state-of-the-art models studied achieve less than 60% accuracy on this ranking task.

The authors derive the ranking accuracy an idealized model would reach if it perfectly optimized the DPO or RLHF objective. Existing models fall substantially short of that idealized level, producing an alignment gap. The analysis attributes this discrepancy to the DPO objective's difficulty correcting even mild ranking mistakes inherited from its reference model, supported by theoretical and empirical evidence.

The paper also derives an efficient formula for measuring how difficult an individual preference example is to learn. Finally, ranking accuracy strongly correlates with win rate when the model remains close to its reference model. That condition is central to the finding and helps clarify differences between on-policy and off-policy preference learning.
neurips-2024-preference-learning-algorit.tldr: Preference-tuned models often rank preferred outputs poorly, and the paper identifies an objective-related gap between observed and idealized ranking accuracy.

paragraphs: Clustered data requires information describing which elements belong together. Random Cycle Coding, or RCC, provides an optimal lossless method for encoding these assignments for arbitrary datasets. Its contribution concerns the storage of assignment information, connecting the encoding of elements with the representation of their cluster memberships.

RCC encodes elements sequentially and communicates assignments through cycles in the permutation determined by their encoding order. It requires no training, and its worst-case computational complexity grows quasi-linearly with the size of the largest cluster. The authors characterize achievable bit rates using the cluster sizes and total number of elements, reporting consistent improvements over earlier methods with less computation and memory.

Experiments in vector databases show savings of up to two bytes per element. RCC also removes the need to assign integer identifiers to vectors, contributing to savings of up to 70% in the reported similarity-search database systems. These are maximum reported savings, illustrating how assignment encoding and identifier storage can materially affect database size.
neurips-2024-random-cycle-coding-lossles.tldr: Random Cycle Coding losslessly compresses cluster assignments without training and achieves substantial storage savings in evaluated vector databases.

paragraphs: Speech dysfluency modeling supports spoken-language learning and speech therapy. SSDM addresses three obstacles identified by the authors: existing solutions scale poorly, large dysfluency corpora are lacking, and an effective learning framework is needed. The paper responds with a combination of alignment methods, simulated training data, and an integrated modeling system.

For alignment, SSDM adopts articulatory gestures as a scalable basis for forced alignment and introduces a connectionist subsequence aligner for dysfluency alignment. These components address how speech and its associated structure are matched. The authors also introduce Libri-Dys, a large simulated dysfluency corpus, directly targeting the shortage of data available for this task.

The final component is an end-to-end system using large language models. Together, the contributions address data availability and the machinery for learning from that data within one framework. The authors express the expectation that SSDM could become a standard for dysfluency modeling; this is a proposed future role for the system rather than a demonstrated adoption outcome.
neurips-2024-ssdm-scalable-speech-dysflu.tldr: SSDM combines new alignment methods, a large simulated dysfluency corpus, and an LLM-based system for scalable speech dysfluency modeling.

paragraphs: In strategic classification, people or other agents can alter observable features to obtain a positive prediction. This paper studies online binary classification when the learner sees only those altered features. A directed graph describes which manipulations are feasible, making the learner's problem depend on both its candidate classifiers and the available feature changes.

The authors introduce Strategic Littlestone Dimension to measure this joint complexity. In the realizable setting, it characterizes instance-optimal mistake bounds for deterministic learners. They also improve regret guarantees in the agnostic setting through a refined reduction that explicitly accounts for the difficulty of not observing agents' original features.

The analysis then relaxes exact knowledge of the manipulation graph: the learner instead knows a family of possible graphs. The authors derive guarantees when all agents use one shared graph from that family, and when manipulation graphs vary adversarially without being consistently described by any single family member. This extends the theory to distinct forms of uncertainty about strategic behavior.
neurips-2024-strategic-littlestone-dimen.tldr: Strategic Littlestone Dimension characterizes deterministic mistake bounds for realizable online classification with manipulated features and supports broader regret analyses.

paragraphs: Turning a simple lead sheet into a rich accompaniment requires tracks to work together and maintain structure over time. This paper tackles those challenges by separating style factors and dividing arrangement into two interpretable stages. The goal is structured, controllable generation with improved computational efficiency.

First, the system retrieves piano texture styles to produce a piano arrangement from the lead sheet. It then introduces orchestral function styles to transform that arrangement into multiple tracks. Vector quantization and a multi-stream Transformer model how orchestration style develops over longer spans, connecting local arrangement choices with the flow of the piece.

Experiments show that this factorization improves both generative capacity and efficiency. The system supports multiple genres and allows style control at different levels of composition. Compared with existing baselines, the authors report better coherence, structure, and overall arrangement quality. These findings support organizing accompaniment generation around distinct musical decisions while modeling their evolution across the resulting arrangement.
neurips-2024-structured-multi-track-acco.tldr: A two-stage style-based system turns lead sheets into coherent multi-track accompaniments with controllable structure and improved efficiency.

paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning requires recognizing both previously seen and unseen classes without being told which group a test image belongs to. TPR addresses this setting using a pretrained vision-language model. It targets both limited feature expressiveness and the loss of unseen-class generalization that can accompany adaptation to seen classes.

The first design aligns visual and linguistic features in two spaces. An additional attribute space is built from a reservoir combining a fixed vocabulary with learnable tokens. These complementary components provide flexible control over feature granularity, helping represent complex visual-language relationships, particularly for fine-grained recognition.

The second design preserves relationships among classes during adaptation. Its objective encourages the combined seen-and-unseen feature structure to resemble CLIP's structure by maintaining pairwise class angles in attribute space. This is intended to retain CLIP's generalization capability. Experiments across twelve object-recognition datasets show TPR outperforming strong prompt-learning and conventional generative zero-shot baselines, supporting the combination of richer alignment and preserved class relationships.
neurips-2024-tpr-topology-preserving-res.tldr: TPR combines an attribute reservoir with preserved class geometry to improve recognition of mixed seen and unseen classes.

paragraphs: Alignment through decoding changes a language model's response distribution without updating its parameters. Principled versions seek an optimal value function that captures how generation choices contribute to a target reward, but that function is usually unavailable. Earlier approximations use the reference model's value function or short-term rewards, which can lead to suboptimal decoding.

Transfer Q-star estimates the optimal value function implicitly through a baseline model already aligned to a reward. Crucially, that baseline reward can differ from the desired target reward. This creates a way to transfer information from an aligned model into decoding for another objective.

The theoretical analysis bounds the gap from optimal performance and identifies a hyperparameter that controls deviation from the pretrained supervised reference model according to user needs. The authors report a substantially smaller suboptimality gap than prior state-of-the-art methods and better coherence, diversity, and quality across synthetic and real datasets. These findings support the proposed transfer mechanism as a practical approximation for reward-directed decoding.
neurips-2024-transfer-q-star-principled-.tldr: Transfer Q-star uses an already aligned baseline model to guide reward-directed decoding, with theoretical bounds and improved empirical generation quality.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model perform tasks using examples supplied in its prompt. Its effectiveness can change with example selection, example order, or formatting. UniBias investigates internal biases behind this prompt brittleness, focusing on components that push predictions toward particular labels.

The authors examine the contributions of individual feedforward-network vectors and attention heads. By interpreting those contributions, they identify components associated with skewed label predictions. UniBias then identifies and eliminates biased vectors and heads during inference. This places the intervention inside the model's computation, extending beyond the external output adjustments discussed in prior work.

Experiments across twelve natural-language-processing datasets show significant improvements in in-context learning performance and reduced prompt brittleness. The reported findings concern label preferences and sensitivity to prompt design in these tasks. They support the idea that examining individual internal components can reveal useful intervention points for making predictions more reliable across different ways of presenting examples and instructions.
neurips-2024-unibias-unveiling-and-mitig.tldr: UniBias removes internal components associated with label bias during inference, improving in-context learning and reducing prompt sensitivity.
